In algebra, an '''analytically irreducible ring''' is a [[local ring]] whose [[completion (ring theory)|completion]] has no [[zero divisor]]s. Geometrically this corresponds to a [[algebraic variety|variety]] with only one analytic branch at a point.

{{harvtxt|Zariski|1948}} proved that if a local ring of an algebraic variety is a [[normal ring]], then it is analytically irreducible. There are many examples of reduced and irreducible local rings that are analytically reducible, such as the local ring of a [[Singular point of a curve|node]] of an irreducible curve, but it is hard to find examples that are also normal. {{harvs|txt|last=Nagata|year1=1958|year2=1962|loc2=Appendix A1, example 7}} gave such an example of a normal [[Noetherian ring|Noetherian]] local ring that is analytically reducible.

==Nagata's example==

Suppose that ''K'' is a field of characteristic not 2, and ''K''&nbsp;{{brackets|''x'',''y''}} is the [[formal power series ring]] over ''K'' in 2 variables. Let ''R'' be the subring of ''K''&nbsp;{{brackets|''x'',''y''}} generated by ''x'', ''y'', and the elements ''z''<sub>''n''</sub> and localized at these elements, where 
:<math>w=\sum_{m>0} a_mx^m</math> is [[transcendental element|transcendental]] over ''K''(''x'')
:<math>z_1=(y+w)^2</math>
:<math>z_{n+1}=(z_1-(y+\sum_{0<m<n}a_mx^m)^2)/x^n</math>.
Then ''R''[''X'']/(''X''<sup> 2</sup>–''z''<sub>1</sub>) is a normal Noetherian local ring that is analytically reducible.
